children: By Jason Wilson

Austrian Grüner Veltliner is the house white at my unassuming local bar in Philadelphia. This would have been unheard of five years ago. Seeing Austria's umlauted signature grape poured for regulars in Eagles jerseys, I feel vindicated.

For more than two decades I've been singing the praises of Grüner Veltliner as the most crowd-pleasing of white wines. Now I've lived long enough to have watched it go from an obscure grape pushed by cool-kid sommeliers to something that's found on most shop shelves and wine lists in the U.S.

Grüner Veltliner seemed to arrive stateside out of nowhere around the turn of the 21st century. Between 2000 and 2024, Austria's global wine exports jumped from around $24 million to $266 million annually, according to the Austrian Wine Marketing Board. But there is still work to do: Italy's wine exports totaled nearly $9 billion last year.

Part of the reason Grüner Veltliner hasn't become as popular as other big-name whites is its unwieldy name (pronounced GROO-ner VELT-lee-ner). In an unfortunate attempt to make the wine happen, winesellers in the aughts started referring to it by the nickname "Groo-Vee." These days, it's not unusual to see it short-handed to "Grüner" (which just means "green," for the green variety of the Veltliner family of grapes.)
As loud as my fellow Philadelphians root for the Eagles, I will keep cheering on Grüner. Here's why it's the rare wine with potential to bridge the divide between tastes.
A wine for all

"Grüner hasn't completely registered with normal people yet, but wine people are fully aware of the incredible array of styles," said Valerie Kathawala, co-founder and co-editor of Trink, a magazine about the wines of Austria and Germany.

White wine fans tend to fall into three camps-Chardonnay drinkers who like rich, full-bodied whites, Sauvignon Blanc sippers who favor acidity and herbaceousness, and Pinot Grigio pounders who prioritize lightness and drinkability. At dinners, I tend to serve Grüner Veltliner, which usually appeals to all three.

The wine can take on different personalities and expressions, depending on where in Austria it's grown. The Wachau, with its fairy-tale hills along the Danube, is Austria's most famous Grüner Veltliner region. But it is just as wonderful when it comes from the limestone soils of Kremstal, Kamptal or Burgenland. The grape is also grown in places like New York's Finger Lakes, the Pacific Northwest and in Eastern Europe, but Austria is where it thrives best.

Grüner can be aromatic or mineral, peppery or spicy, but it's always lively, with big flavor that doesn't veer into overly fruity territory. Sometimes it resembles the love child of Sauvignon Blanc and Viognier. Other times it veers Riesling-like, especially as it ages. At its best, it can follow down the path of a very good Chardonnay that's mineral and has good acidity-not that oaky, buttery stuff that turned you against the grape.
The famed Wachau winemaker Emmerich Knoll once told me: "You can taste 10 Grüner Veltliners and still cannot say, 'I know what Grüner Veltliner tastes like.' "
Reliable at all prices
At my local, the house Grüner is $8 a glass, or $6 during happy hour.
Unlike so much Pinot Noir or California Chardonnay, with Grüner Veltliner, you can find good quality and value at all price levels, and spending more will generally elevate the experience.

That takes a lot of risk out of the buying experience: If your budget is $15, you can get solid liters of Grüner for under that. At $25, you hit a sweet spot that includes a variety of super-good options; jumping to around $50 will bring excellent single-vineyard special bottlings into your budget.
A friend to every meal
Grüner Veltliner's relatively high acidity, herbal-fruity profile and signature white pepper notes help it pair with everything from barbecue to mole to sashimi to pad thai to fried chicken.
I especially love how it mingles with non-meat dishes, like root vegetables or beet salads, and have put it to the test with notoriously hard-to-pair ingredients like Brussels sprouts and artichokes.
Grüner Veltliner is a lot like the perfect party guest: approachable, chatty and good in a crowd, yet mysteriously intriguing on first meeting-a stranger you want to know better.
Four faces of Grüner
For the Pinot Grigio pounder: Mantlerhof Grüner Veltliner, $25 for 1-liter bottle

Crisp, with notes of green apple and ripe pear and a kiss of pepper and herbs, it pairs with everything from seafood to salad to schnitzel. Everyone loves a liter, which carries about an extra two glasses over the standard 750 mL bottle.
For the Sauvignon Blanc sipper: Gobelsburg Grüner Veltliner, $20
Lively, zingy acidity, with notes of grapefruit and herbs. Try it with grilled fish.
For Sancerre or white Bordeaux fans: Knoll Ried Loibner Federspiel, $32
This ageworthy bottling delivers big acidity, with notes of lime zest, white blossom, tangerine and grilled lemon. It has an underlying saltiness and a crisp mineral finish.
For white Burgundy drinkers: Alzinger Ried Steinertal Smaragd, $84

This is the rich, complex style of Grüner. Elegant and structured, it has juicy acidity and aromas of jasmine, hay and spice. With flavors of pear, melon, nutmeg, the wine has a long finish and pairs with just about everything.
